problem: The step says the 12 kN load and the link force at B have a resultant that 'is not along AB'. With the numbers of this very problem the link force on B is (−9, +12) kN, so the resultant with the (0, −12) kN load is (−9, 0) kN — exactly along AB. The stated reason for AB not being a two-force member is therefore false, though the conclusion (analyse AB as its own free body) is right.
fix: Give the correct reason: three forces act on AB — the reaction at A, the 12 kN load at B and the link force at B — so AB fails the two-force test (a two-force member has forces at exactly two points and nothing else). Do not claim the resultant at B lies off the axis; with these numbers it is 9 kN along AB, so AB ends up carrying only axial force.

problem: Step 8 says the reaction at A 'does not point along AB's own axis'. AB is horizontal and the reaction came out as 9 kN horizontal, so it does lie along AB. The sentence contradicts the arithmetic two lines above and will confuse a student. The chapter's own three-force rule (Section 3) also proves the reaction must lie along AB: the 12 kN load and the link force both pass through B, so the third force, the reaction at A, must pass through B too.
fix: Reaction at A = 9 kN horizontal to the right, that is, along AB itself. By the three-force concurrency rule this was forced: the load and the link force meet at B, so the reaction at A must also pass through B. The vertical component is zero.

problem: 'Assuming a pin reaction is vertical, or lies along the member. Here A_y comes out exactly zero; a wrong assumption would have hidden that.' The two wrong assumptions are not equal: assuming the reaction lies along the member gives the correct answer in this problem, so nothing is exposed. Only the 'vertical reaction' assumption fails (it makes ΣFx impossible).
fix: Keep only the vertical assumption as the warning: assuming the reaction at A is vertical forces A_x = 0, which contradicts ΣFx = 0 and exposes the error at once. Add that in this geometry the reaction does lie along AB, so this example cannot catch the 'along the member' guess.

problem: Example 2 is Example 1 rescaled, and quiz Q3 repeats Example 2 number for number; both examples again give A_y = 0. Every illustration in the chapter therefore shows a frame member with zero vertical reaction, so students never see the general case where the pin reaction has two nonzero components.
fix: Change one case so the vertical reaction is not zero — for example keep AB = 3 m with C 4 m above A but put the 12 kN load at the midpoint of AB instead of at B. Then A_y ≠ 0, AB really carries bending, and the free-body method shows its value. Give quiz Q3 different numbers from the worked example.
